title: A commenter rewrote my RSI rules and tripled the return, and the win rate dropped from 77% to 42%
author: person-person12
selftext:
I ran a plain RSI test and posted it. Buy SPY when RSI(14) closes under 30, sell when it closes back above 50, daily candles, nothing else in it. 35 trades since 2000, 27 of them won, and it still finished well behind just holding the thing.

Somebody in the comments said the exit was the problem, that 48 to 100 is where price actually trends and selling at 50 cuts off the part you were waiting for. He gave five rules instead:

1. buy when daily RSI is under 30
2. sell if price closes below your buy price
3. sell if RSI falls under 52 after being above 70
4. buy back if RSI rises over 52
5. sell if it breaks under 49

So i coded his version and ran it on the same candles. SPY daily, 3 January 2000 to 30 March 2026, 6,599 candles, 100k account, commission and slippage charged on both sides of every trade.

**His rules:** +179.2%, 412 trades, **41.8% win rate**, profit factor 1.54, max drawdown 34.8%

**My rules:** +53.2%, 35 trades, **77.1% win rate**, profit factor 2.12, max drawdown 29.3%

**Holding SPY:** +340.2%, max drawdown 56.5%

He was right about the exit. Three and a half times the return out of the same indicator, and the piece that paid for it was rule 4, buying back in over 52 instead of sitting in cash waiting for another sub 30 print. The 35 trade version spends most of 26 years flat.

The win rate going from 77% to 42% is the part id want anybody looking at their own results to sit with. Same indicator, same market, same window, and the version that won less than half its trades made three times the money. A win rate on its own doesnt tell you which of these two youre holding, and the profit factor doesnt either, because his is the lower of the two.

Both of them finish behind holding SPY over the window, which i dont think is a knock on either rule set. 56% drawdown is what holding cost you and 35% is what his cost, so he gave up roughly half the return to take about a third less pain.

The SPY history i test on in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) starts in 2000, so this is one window with three sets of rules laid over it and no stitching. The reason his version could be tested at all is that he wrote it out as five conditions with numbers in them. "sell when momentum fades" isnt testable, "sell if RSI falls under 52 after being above 70" is.

comments.author: ciaranwalsh96
comments.body:
The return comparison would be much more informative with two implementation details: is the SPY series total-return adjusted for dividends, and does cash earn interest while the strategy is flat? Over 26 years, both can materially change the gap between an intermittently invested strategy and buy-and-hold.



The five-rule version also needs a genuinely untouched period now. Those thresholds were proposed after someone saw the original result, so the same 2000–2026 window is still in-sample for the redesign even if the code itself is fixed. Freeze the rules here, then report the next 6–12 months separately or run a walk-forward test where each rule set only trades data that came after it was chosen.



For comparison, I’d show CAGR, time in market, volatility or Sortino, max drawdown, and return over maximum drawdown alongside the win rate. That would test the real claim: whether giving up return bought enough reduction in risk and exposure.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Both fair questions. The SPY series is **price only**, so dividends arent in either number, and cash earns nothing while the strategy sits flat. Both of those corrections move the comparison toward holding rather than toward the strategy.

On the window, agreed. The five rule version is in-sample and I'd rather freeze it there than re-report the same 2000 to 2026 run and call it a second test.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that you tested the commenter's rules exactly as written, and the point about testable conditions is the real lesson. One caution is that his version was found after seeing results on the same window, so I'd treat 179% as in-sample until it's checked on a period neither of you used (another index, or the data before 2000). With 412 trades in 26 years, the trades cluster into a few trends and selloffs, so counting episodes would be more honest. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for tagging which crises or shocks drove the drawdowns.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Youre right that its in-sample. The rules came after seeing the result on that window so I'm not going to call 179% anything else until it runs on data neither of us looked at.

Counting episodes instead of trades is the better point tbh. 412 trades across 26 years is maybe a dozen real regimes wearing a big sample size.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That's the right way to hold it, and a dozen real regimes is a fair way to size the evidence. I'll look out for the out-of-sample run. Thanks for taking the points on board.

comments.author: LatterRain5
comments.body:
1. Win rate don't matter more than profit factor. So check pf first then wr.
2. Daily candle? Why? Less noise or no noise?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right, and thats basically the whole post, the **42% version made more money than the 77% one.** Daily was only because the first test I posted was daily and I wanted the rewrite tested on the same thing, noise wasnt the reason. What would you have run it on?
